en: Commentary on the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*,
composed by Bodhisattva Dharmapāla;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
If one says that this can enable those with poisonous wisdom to become human,
so as to cause their insight to be utterly clear and to eliminate their evils— having paid homage with respect, I shall now contemplate its meaning.
The treatise states:

Those who assert that there are consciousnesses such as visual consciousness do so because [consciousness] is the fruit of observation regarding things to be discarded or things to be accepted, whereby one either relinquishes or grasps them.
The entity to be abandoned and the cause of perversion are what are being demonstrated here.

In this context, the word "etc. (ādi) includes the five types of consciousness based on the sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*) as accepted by others, because others invariably maintain that these are real entities serving as their respective objects.
Mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not like this, for it is not invariably so;
it is admitted to exist conventionally because it takes objects such as chariots as its conditions.

Even if one were to grant that mental consciousness has a partial aspect that takes real entities as its objects, it is still able to take a semblance of those [realities] as its object, even when separated from their actual presence.
Once the objects of the visual and other consciousnesses are established as being inseparable from them, they are then fully established; therefore, no further effort is required here.

Furthermore, because the forms cognized by the wisdom resulting from habitual cultivation are certainly not within the domain of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and because they are established exactly as they are perceived.

Now, this refers only to the objects of the wisdoms produced through hearing, reflection, and innate acquisition; thus, the objects perceived by such mental consciousness are entirely non-existent, because they cannot take their own constituent aggregates as objects, and furthermore, because they take past and future things—which are not real entities—as objects, just like unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
These words include the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).
If that is so, how is it with the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) that is induced by those sense organs and their respective consciousnesses?
It is not the case that this [mental consciousness] arises simultaneously with or immediately after them, for it takes as its objects (ālambana) forms and other phenomena that have already ceased.
Alternatively, it might take the present as its object; however, this is not possible because such an object has never been apprehended by the sensory consciousnesses.

This would mean that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) could directly perceive the essential nature of external objects on its own, which would result in the absurdity that there are no deaf or blind people, and furthermore, it would contradict inferential cognition (*anumāna*).
The acknowledgment that there is a distinct faculty serves to exclude the increase of matter (*rūpa*), as this is what is intended;

however, no such consideration applies to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because the various consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, only arise when matter serves as their objective support and condition.
Since non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is by nature merely the state of non-action, it is admitted by [the opponent] himself to be non-existent; this was the original intention.

To claim that this [non-informative matter] would serve as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to its object is to fall deeply into an erroneous path, because it would then be of the nature of an apprehended object (*grāhya*).
With this correct intention, one first negates its nature as an object (*ālambana*); by means of that same reasoning, one then negates its nature as a support (*āśraya*).
At the same time, the sense organs and the functional matter (*rūpa*) [of the faculties] will be provisionally admitted.
Regarding the term "external objects" (*bāhyārtha*): they maintain that there exist distinct objects apart from these [consciousnesses].
This [term] reveals their error; it is called "objects" because it reveals that they cling to the existence of separate entities that can be apprehended.
How could it be said that [the object] is a composite whole?
Since it is not a composite whole, it is logical that it is a real entity (*dravya*).
Indeed, as you have challenged me, your own position is internally inconsistent; what fault, then, do I incur?

Since it is accepted that [cognition] arises by depending on both its actual object and the collection as a whole, we shall temporarily set aside this objection while intending to state its specific faults. Or, let us grant for the sake of argument that atoms exist;

even though atoms are seen to arise and perish only when aggregated, each atom as a substantial entity depends [on its own parts], rather than depending on the collection as a whole, just like visible form and other such phenomena.

Even if all the sense faculties were to manifest simultaneously and their objects were not confused, because the functional capacities of those faculties are each determined, they would possess the ability to discern individual real entities; for each and every atom would constitute an objective referent (*ālambana*), as it is the nature of that cause.

Because they are the causal nature (*hetutva*) of those consciousnesses such as visual consciousness, they are the meaning of being the immediate constituent parts (*sākṣāt-aṅga*) for their arising. However,

some say that the objects of cognition (*ālambana-viṣaya*) are the causes for the arising of consciousness because they exist among the various conditions (*pratyaya*), or because they constitute the collective aggregate (*saṃghāta*) therein.
Those theorists maintain that the collection of all atoms constitutes the objective referent (*ālambana*) because consciousness arises with that as its characteristic mark.
Since cognition arises with respect to the aggregate as a whole, it is certain that this [aggregate] is the objective referent.
As it is said:
"If consciousness possesses that image, then that is its object.
Both of these theorists maintain that the image must accord with this principle.

If the reason is not stated, this reason lacks an example; it is just as when the nature of atoms as a collective generality—which serves as the objective condition (ālambana) for the production of [cognitions] such as "cause" and so forth—is established.

Furthermore, if one admits that one does not apprehend the real entity (vastu) external to consciousness, there would necessarily be the fallacy of a contradiction between the subject and its own nature (dharmasvabhāvavirodha).
However, Dignāga does not admit this; rather, this point is universally accepted even by his opponents, and it is therefore employed as an analogy.
If it were merely as stated, one would have to apply it directly to the thesis (*sādhya*) being established.
The intention of the preceding formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is this:

the two reasons (*hetu*) presented in the treatise are merely "indicative reasons" (*upalakṣaṇa-hetu*) and thus do not constitute [valid] reasons in themselves. Because there is no commonly accepted example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is necessary to set forth the corresponding reason (*anurūpa-hetu*) for this purpose.
Why is this so? Furthermore, it is to demonstrate that the principle one has argued is free from error, clarifying that others commonly agree to posit a fifth category [of sound].

Even if it were granted as a reason (*hetu*), it would be like the common agreement that all non-existent things lack the nature of existence; thus, it is not a reason, just as atoms are not [the cause of sound].

Furthermore, even if one were to grant that the atoms themselves constitute the nature of the cause, it is still said that they do not possess the nature of the object (ālambana), because the characteristics of the atoms are not the characteristics of that [object]. Thus, it is said that for the sense-consciousnesses, the atoms are not the objective domain.

Regarding the statement "like the sense-faculties": just as the sense-faculties, although they are indeed the direct supporting causes for consciousness, do not constitute its objects because they lack the characteristics of an object, so too it is with atoms.
Regarding the statement, "Those things that lack its characteristic are not its objects," what does this mean? It is said in response:
"That which is called its 'object' (*viṣaya*) and so forth.
As for "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), it refers to that which is cognized as either a specific or a general characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa* or *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
What is concentration?
Is this, moreover, called "understanding" (*vidyā*)?
It is so because it arises in the manner of those [preceding] characteristics.
The meaning of this statement is that consciousness arises with an appearance identical to that [object], because it conforms to its substance.
This is what is called "cognizing that object"; yet in reality, apart from consciousness, is there any distinct cognized object that could serve as the causal nature for that consciousness?

However, when there is merely the appearance of an external object, which is arranged before oneself like a reflection in a mirror, it is commonly accepted that this constitutes the cognition of that object.
However, consciousness does not conform to the individual self-nature of each atom.

Therefore, although these atoms serve as the objective basis (ālambana-vastu), even if they possess the nature of a cause, they do not function as causes in this context; thus, like the sense organs, they are not objects of cognition despite having the nature of a cause.

If it is admitted that [the cause] functions as an object of cognition by virtue of being a cause, then the sense faculties (*indriya*) would likewise be such objects; thus, they too would become [the objects of cognition].
This statement refers back to the previously mentioned principle regarding their association; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*).
However, this implies that the nature of the cause is not itself the objective aspect (nimitta) of its faculty.
If, as you have stated, the cause is to serve as the probans (sādhana), then by virtue of being that cause, does it become the objective aspect?
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*), there is also the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). If this were the case, what would be the meaning of "not having that characteristic"?
It is to clarify the establishment of one's own thesis; for one's own position is not established merely by stating the faults of another's position.
This statement is intended to demonstrate that [the object] is not itself capable of producing the aspect of its own consciousness,
for the object is not composed of atoms, just like the eye and other sense organs.
If the phrase "being the causal nature of that" were used, it would serve as the proponent’s preliminary establishment of another's position to clarify what is commonly accepted by others.
At this point, the intention is to refute the opponent and establish one's own position; thus, these words are set forth.
The thesis (pakṣa) is intended to definitively establish that [position], rather than leaving it uncertain for the sake of the opponent’s school, for fear that they might not accept it.

The aforementioned "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) reason, which fails to establish [the thesis] for the opponent, is itself a refutation; why then rely on one's own school’s further formal inference (anumāna)?

Generally speaking, what is called "inconclusive" does not necessarily mean it is definitively unestablished; rather, it is feared that doubt may arise. For this reason, it is necessary to formulate a formal inference once more.

Alternatively, if it is argued that this [consciousness] does not possess the characteristics of those [atoms], then its nature as a definitive cognition regarding the atoms would not be established; for "definitive cognition" refers to the arising of a consciousness according to its object's characteristics.
Since those [characteristics] are absent, it is clear that there is no basis for this being a definitive cognition, and one should rather say it lacks the nature of definitive cognition.
This reason alone is not a valid object-condition (*ālambana*), just like the atoms of the sense faculties.

Others further distinguish between the various consciousnesses to demonstrate that visual consciousness cannot cognize atomic forms, because those [atomic] characteristics are absent, just as in the case of the consciousnesses of the other sense faculties.
In the same way, regarding the other consciousnesses, one should reverse this and state that they are "like the sense organs" (*indriya*); thus, the term *yāna* (vehicle) is indeed appropriate.
As for the specific metaphor, it must be sought by inferring its meaning from this principle.
Furthermore, even if the term were used in the sense of "causal nature," it would be rendered useless.
Although that [object] functions as a cause, it does not possess the nature of being an object-condition (*ālambana*).
This case is likewise: while it is indeed functional, no atom (*paramāṇu*) of sound or other [sensory objects] can be the cause for the arising of consciousness through another sense-faculty.
Some say that because no aggregation appears within the very substance of consciousness, it cannot be an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just as the atoms of the sense organs (*indriya*) are not.

This is because the nature of an object consists in the arrangement of its phenomenal characteristics (*ākāra*) within consciousness; since such [an arrangement] does not exist here [in consciousness itself], it is not an object.
In principle, it is said that there is no manifestation of an aggregate.

This has been stated provisionally; for *paramāṇu* (atoms) cannot be the object of cognition, because their status as a logical probans (*sādhana*) is inconsistent, and because their nature as an objective domain (*viṣayatva*) is not well-established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If that is so, then the aggregate as a whole is the object.
However, regarding all the proofs (sādhana) mentioned, if they are examined against the Mīmāṃsaka position, they all possess the nature of being unestablished (asiddha).
This is indeed the logical reality; nevertheless, the aggregate exists substantially with those characteristics and can thus be the focal object (ālambana).
Because it lacks a cause, the consciousness of those individual characteristics cannot produce the consciousness of their collective aggregate; thus, the aggregate does not arise.
Since that [aggregate] does not arise, how can this consciousness cause one to perceive that [aggregate] as its object?
Because the characteristics of the object of cognition (ālambana) are incompatible [with that], it does not possess the meaning of being an object of cognition.
For this reason, what was stated previously—
that the principle of their compatibility is established— is here shown to be untenable.
If that is so, what is the characteristic of the object-condition (*ālambana-nimitta*)?
Whatever constitutes an object must, by principle, give rise to a cognition that resembles its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
That cognition which arises in accordance with the object is the producer, and that [object] is the object-condition.
Some say that for something to function as an object (*ālambana*), it must logically be the cause for the arising of the mind and its mental factors.
Once these have arisen, they experience the object accordingly and engage in verbal designation; at that time, it is termed an "object of cognition" (*ālambana-viṣaya*).

If an object possesses these two characteristics, only then can it be properly designated as an "object-condition" (ālambana), meaning it is an objective sphere that has the nature of producing [cognition].
Citing the Āgama, this is precisely what is meant by the "nature of being a condition for arising."
Because it is the cause for the arising [of consciousness], that which is commonly accepted as the condition for the arising of that consciousness is its object;
since the manifestation of its own essential nature serves no purpose in this context, it is not mentioned.
The collection as a whole cannot be the producer because it is not a real entity.
Since this collection is not a real entity, it is impossible to describe its nature as being either identical to or different from the constituents that comprise it.
Furthermore, there is no unreal thing that possesses the functional capacity to produce an effect, just as in the case of a second moon.
Just as a second moon cannot produce the cognition of the appearance of a second moon.
If that is so, for what reason does this appearance arise?
It is because the sense organ is impaired.

When the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is damaged by its clarity being obstructed by cataracts or the like, one perceives two moons arising from the very location of that impaired faculty; this is not because it is a real object.
Therefore, although that image may exist during these two months, it is not the object of this consciousness.
Just as with a second moon, even if this consciousness possesses its image, it is not designated as the object because it does not arise [as a real entity].

This is because a general aggregate such as "existence" (sattā), which lacks substantial reality, is not the cause for the arising of consciousness; since it lacks substantial reality, it is like a second moon.
It is precisely for this reason that it is established as not being a cause, and thus it is not an object of cognition, just like a second moon.

Furthermore, by means of this second analogy of the moon, one should understand that the fault of indeterminacy (*anaikāntika*) is stated regarding those [arguments] based on mutual causality (*anyonyahetu*).
Moreover, because the meaning of consciousness is established through reasoning, the fault is contradictory (*viruddha*).

Furthermore, visual consciousness does not take as its object the atoms of the aggregation of blue and so forth, because their substance is not of a nature that arises [as such], just like the consciousnesses of the other sense organs.
This analogy is commonly accepted, and thus it is not stated separately.
Because the second moon analogy is not a real entity, it should be understood that this establishes its status as a non-cause.
As it has been said: "Even though it possesses the nature of having characteristics, it is not an object [of cognition]"; this statement further signifies that it is not its cause.
If one says there is no second moon, how is it that two forms are currently perceived?

It is because, once internal predispositions (*śakti*) have been distributed according to their specific differences, a consciousness resembling those forms subsequently arises; this is just like seeing objects arise during a dream. Due to this, one falsely constructs such an understanding, and while looking at the actual moon, one perceives another [form] superimposed upon it.

Some say that when both [moons] appear simultaneously within the visual consciousness, because it is difficult to definitively establish their sequence, they are treated as occurring at once; subsequently, following these two images, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) then says, "I see a second moon."
Or again, some may say:
"There is an error in the number [of moons] as commonly perceived, due to a defect in the sense faculty.

If one considers this from the perspective of a school that does not admit external objects, such various perceptions are merely false attachments. For how could a mental consciousness—which arises immediately following a visual consciousness that lacks an external object as its objective support—simultaneously apprehend two forms and produce such an understanding as seeing two moons?

Furthermore, regarding sounds and so forth, if the consciousnesses that take them as objects were unable to discern their sequence, would there not result two simultaneous perceptions of sound and so on?

Even for a person with excellent eyesight, the successive order of mental consciousness is already difficult to discern; how much more so for a consciousness dependent on the material sense-faculties to perceive their distinctions—this would inevitably result in many instances of perceiving two forms simultaneously.

Furthermore, Cāṇḍāla, if you claim that time exists as a real entity apart from consciousness, why do you needlessly and falsely add two months, asserting that there is a confusion within the calculation of numbers?
Apart from consciousness, the grasping at two kinds of atoms—whether as individual units or as a collective aggregate—is entirely lacking in one part of its definition.
Furthermore, as previously explained, by the force of the principles of proof and refutation, taking these as objects results in a lack of correspondence, because they are deficient in one part.
The manifestation of its own essential nature and its capacity to produce [cognition]—only when these two factors are present does something qualify as an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
At the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), the first factor is lacking; at the second extreme [of a single moment], the second factor is lost.
If it were so, then the two kinds of faults previously discussed would be further gathered and reconciled to ensure there is no discrepancy.

Some say that regarding the characteristic of aggregation (*saṃcita-lakṣaṇa*), each atom (*paramāṇu*) possesses its own characteristic of aggregation; it is precisely through this accumulation of atoms (*saṃcitaparamāṇu*) that a characteristic appears.
According to the number of atoms present, whether many or few, all of these truly exist.
Since a collective appearance arises in the location of the atoms, and because it possesses its own specific characteristics and a real nature, it must be an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
This is because both [components] are existent.
Thus, regarding what has already been established previously, there is no way to proceed further.
Is the characteristic of aggregation identical to the atom, or is it not?
Since objects possess many characteristics by virtue of their various meanings, these atoms are asserted to have both atomic form and a composite form.
How could it be reasonable for these two characteristics to coexist within a single entity?

There are many characteristics; all composite things that possess form have the four great elements—earth and so forth—as their nature. Each of these possesses its own superior capacity by way of intrinsic nature, such that characteristics like blue, yellow, and so on are distinguished according to the object and the sense faculty.
That is to say, within those many characteristics of location, there exists a collective characteristic at the point of the atom (*paramāṇu*).
Since this very characteristic serves as the objective domain for the visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions, it possesses the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If this is so, why do you not state that consciousness has a collective aspect within its subtle locations?
Since particles have a collective aspect, why do you not likewise state that consciousness has a collective aspect?

Therefore, it is further stated that within the subtle [atoms] there exists a collective aggregate; this very statement serves as a skillful means to also reveal that consciousness possesses the collective aspect of the atoms.
If that is so, and if each individual atom possesses these characteristics, why then is it further described as having "collective characteristics"? [The answer is:
It is accepted in this treatise that a mass of form consists of many atoms when analyzed; it is precisely because of this that it has the nature of a collective aggregate.
It is not substantially existent, as has already been stated previously; why labor to repeat it?
There is another underlying intention.

Even if things were substantially real with distinct individual essences, these characteristics can only be known by relying upon one another at the point of their aggregation; thus, it is said that observing the characteristic of aggregation involves nothing else.

Furthermore, even if all existing things were by nature an aggregation of atoms, there would still be distinctions of superiority and inferiority among individual phenomena; when observing these according to their specific natures, for instance, the color blue constitutes the earth element.
Such explanations are indeed reasonable.
Even granting this, just as when an extremely red object first arises, many factors are so powerful that no space remains;
yet this argument is made based on the possibility of such space existing.
If that is so, how can it be said that atoms are not seen by the sense faculties? Furthermore, how is it that only "suchness-knowing" (*tathatā-jñāna*) can see atoms?

Because the characteristic of the object (*viṣaya-nimitta*) is not the referent of consciousness, nor is it the objective domain of consciousness based on the sense faculties; therefore, it is said to be "not of the sense faculties. That which is not of the sense faculties is observed solely by "suchness-knowing."
Furthermore, by what reasoning is it evident that while atoms are perceived, their gross forms are not seen—just as hardness and so forth, or as hardness and moisture and so forth?

Even if such entities as blue and so forth exist therein, they are not the objective domain of visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions, because the functional capacities of the sense organs are each restricted to their respective objects.
The same applies to dust; there is no contradiction with what is commonly accepted. Is it not the case that the subtle lacks the nature of solidity because its substance is distinct?
Regarding this thesis, since it is accepted that the ten locations are merely the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), these words are without fault.

However, as has already been stated: for you who perceive jars, bowls, and so forth, and for you who realize them in such a manner, the jar and the bowl would consequently become objects of sensory perception (*indriya-vijñāna*).

When viewed through their similarity, because cognition does not deviate from its own respective object, and because sensory perception arises in accordance with the presently existing object, there is no distinction between the cognition and the object.
How is this known?
It is because such verbal designations as "jar" or "bowl" do not refer to any distinct entities among the atoms within them.

Rather, the atoms take their collective aggregation as their object. Indeed, at the time one discerns the intrinsic nature of those jars and so forth, there is no separate fragment within the manifold aggregate; for apart from the actual characteristics of those real entities, no distinct entity of an "aggregation" can be found. Consequently, the sensory consciousnesses apprehending them possess identical mental images without distinction, and it is by virtue of this that the intrinsic nature of the object itself constitutes the status of being the objective condition (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no distinct characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) serving as the condition for its thorough examination, because its nature is subject to different interpretations,

just as in the case of perceiving blue and so forth. If one argues that the characteristics are distinct— where "distinct" refers to differences in shape and arrangement, such as the various forms of the neck, belly, and base of a jar or a small bowl— then [the following applies]:
It is indeed reasonable that cognition differs according to the distinction of its objects;
however, such is not the case here, for there is no difference in the atoms within the objective domain perceived by the sensory consciousnesses.
However, this aggregate is a *saṃvṛti* (conventional reality), and it has already been refuted that such an aggregate is an object of the sensory consciousnesses.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to argue that there is some distinct non-object which causes a difference in the aspects (*ākāra*) of the consciousness.
Furthermore, how do we know that distinct spatial configurations do not exist within the locations of atoms?
It is because the form and characteristics of atoms themselves possess no differentiation.
For any entity that possesses constituent parts, there must necessarily be distinct configurations manifesting across various spatial directions.

However, since the essence of atoms has no spatial dimensions and reaches the ultimate limit of minuteness, how could there ever be any distinction of shape? This remains so even when objects such as jars or bowls differ in their physical forms.
Yet their ultimate circularity has never been different, for they are of one essence without increase or decrease.
Therefore, it is certain that within the aggregate, they do not exist as substantial entities.
Whatever possesses spatial orientation, arrangement, or shape is entirely beyond the range of the sensory faculties and consciousness.
The numerous objections raised above are intended to demonstrate that [the object] possesses distinct characteristics.
The cognition of a jar, a bowl, or the like does not take a distinct entity as its objective referent, just as the cognitions of *sukha* (pleasure) and *duḥkha* (pain) do not.
However, since atoms (*paramāṇu*) are not distinct entities, this demonstrates that they lack the nature of being such objective referents.

If it is argued that linguistic differences arise because their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ, this statement intends to show that the previous claim—that [words] do not take non-distinct things as their objects—is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
His intention in saying this is that although atoms as objects are in fact no different, they are distinguished because their shapes and characteristics are distinct.
That atoms are not different is something we both agree upon.
This is an established conclusion, because there is no distinction among the various atoms (*paramāṇu*).
This demonstrates that distinct entities constitute distinct objects; thus, the answer is not already established.

Alternatively, this clarifies that the consciousnesses of the sense faculties do not have the nature of atomic characteristics with respect to jars, bowls, and so forth, and therefore they are not their objective supports (*ālambana*), just like other types of consciousness.
Other consciousnesses—namely, the mental consciousness or the consciousnesses of the other sense organs—perceive only blue at that time because no yellow aspect is present.

Although the substance of the atoms is manifold, they lack differentiation; yet, because the various sense-consciousnesses possess differentiated aspects, this [perception] is thus established collectively.
Regarding the verse on the nature of not being the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*), the discussion concerning the term "distinction" is the same as in the previous question and answer.
If it is granted that a composite aggregate can conceal its individual characteristics, then the principle that shape (*saṃsthāna*) is not a real object can be established.
Such a superior principle ought to be established.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is devoid of atoms and so forth, just as it is devoid of those [aggregates], then that cognition would simply not exist, just like [the cognition of] an army and the like.
This statement that "jars and the like are not real entities" is due to their being non-substantial things.
This demonstrates that the various non-realities asserted by other schools do not all abandon those contradictory things, just as in the case of sound and so forth.

The cognition of blue is not [the cognition of] non-existence; these two forms and characteristics are distinct. This is because it is a concealed existence (*saṃvṛtisat*), taking jars and the like as its objective nature (*ālambanabhāva*).

Although many different views and logical arguments have been adduced, they ultimately fail to demonstrate that the substantial entity (*dravyasvabhāva*) of the atom possesses any differentiation. Based on the nature of the internal object, one asserts the objective referent (*ālambanavastu*) of one’s own school.

If one were to universally deny the existence of an objective referent (*ālambana*), there would be the fault of contradicting worldly consensus and one's own tenets, for the four types of conditions (*pratyaya*) are taught in the Sūtras.
Here, the term "internal" (*ādhyātmika*) is used to indicate that the referent does not exist apart from consciousness.

Regarding the "substance of the object" (*ālambana-vastu*): this refers to the apprehended portion (*grāhya-bhāga*), which signifies the meaning of consciousness transforming itself into the appearance of an object.
Nevertheless, it exists as if distinguished and situated outside of consciousness, intended to serve as the object.
The fault of contradicting worldly convention remains as before.
Since all worldly people commonly agree that objects exist externally, one should say they are "like external things. However, these do not exist apart from consciousness;

rather, it is the apprehended portion [of consciousness] that appears as if external, leading one to think, "I perceive an object," and thus giving rise to the conceit of a self. This is indeed the cause.

Just as when hair and the like appear in visual consciousness, although external objects do not exist—meaning that no real object exists externally because it is not cognized as such—if one investigates through reasoning, its own essence cannot be determined to reside definitively outside;
even if one were to concede that those external forms truly exist, they would still not be the conditions for consciousness, because they lack the nature of being such [objects].
When the appearance of atoms manifests as if they were external objects, this very [appearance] is its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because it is associated with that image.
As for the phrase "because it accords with the principle of the image," this means "this is precisely this," just as in the case of a causal nature (*hetutva*) and so forth.

Because it accords with the principle of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it further reveals the distinct essential nature of the object of cognition (*ālambana*). As it is said, "consciousness possesses that aspect," this clarifies that one does not depend upon external things as objects; rather, the aspects of the object arise in accordance with what is conceptualized by the mind.

Furthermore, regarding what is conceptually grasped by the mind: since it does not exist externally apart from consciousness, these objective appearances are fundamentally not separate from consciousness; for this reason, they are termed "internal objective appearances."

In this context, the term "internal" implies that sound is not separate from consciousness; since there was originally no such thing as an external object, with respect to what could it be considered internal?
Furthermore, [the internal arises] from this, and only when this exists does it arise.

Alternatively, it may be understood that from this [consciousness], by means of the seventh and fifth [consciousnesses], because their meanings are distinct, consciousness cannot exist apart from its object; therefore, only when this [object] exists does consciousness arise.
The fifth [category] is not mentioned because it is subsumed within the two dharmas.

By clarifying its object (*ālambana*), the logical principle is established, thereby manifesting the probans (*sādhana*). This, then, takes only the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as its probans.
If there is a distinction, it is that the *pramāṇa* (the means of valid cognition) does not depend on external objects, but manifests within the state of dreaming.

As it is said, two factors constitute a single *sādhana* (probans): the consciousness possessing that [object's] aspect and the arising of that consciousness; through these two functions, a single valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established.

Furthermore, even granting for the sake of argument that internal aspects (ākāra) exist, since one perceives only external objects as having falsely appearing aspects, it is said that there are no earth-aspects.

Just as when the mind conceives of an object, its reception arises, and the characteristics of that object are arrayed within [the cognition], which is taken to be reasonable—how could such a part of that [cognition] serve as a co-arising condition?

Since the grasped aspect is absent when the consciousness is separated [from its object], if that very same portion were to give rise to consciousness once again, it would result in the fallacy of contradicting its own nature.

Furthermore, because it remains of that same portion-nature, like the grasping portion, it would consequently fail to possess the nature of being a producer; rather, it would arise merely through the defilement of consciousness by external appearances.

This means that the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) and consciousness arise simultaneously; it is not that two things existing at the same time possess the nature of cause and effect, like the two horns of an ox.
Furthermore, it is not that two non-different things existing at the same time are spoken of in combination by using the term "concomitant" (saha).
Nor is it the case that the object exists as something distinct from consciousness; how, then, can this be called "concomitance"?
In reality, it is thus; however, by the power of the differentiation of their characteristics, one conjectures them to be distinct and expresses them as such.
Because there is a distinction between the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*), this consciousness consequently possesses differentiation.

If this were the case, then the nature of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) would also be merely that which is grasped; it would not be a thing possessing an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) through conceptual construction. This would result in its being a non-genuine objective condition, which contradicts the reason [for its existence]. This is because the meaning of "condition" is commonly accepted even for other grasped differentiated objects, such as when a consciousness of the same class (*sabhāga-vijñāna*) acts as a delimiter at the moment immediately following its cessation (*samanantara-niruddha*); in such cases, this consciousness also functions as a condition by way of four kinds of multiple conditions.
Commentary on the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*, One Fascicle.
